newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge stops deportation of Nicaraguans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge stops deportation of Nicaraguans.

text.p: A U.S. federal judge on Tuesday issued a preliminary injunction to prevent the deportation of thousands of Nicaraguan and other immigrants in three states.
The ruling effectively prevents the U.S. government from sending home Nicaraguans who have lived in legal limbo since coming to the United States during the 1980s civil war in their country.
U.S. District Judge James Lawrence King, in a 67-page ruling that affects immigrants in Florida, Georgia and Alabama, also set a trial date of Jan. 5, 1998 in the case.

"The court finds...that the plaintiff class members have demonstrated their entitlement to preliminary injunctive relief," King wrote, adding that the injunction was needed to prevent "irreparable injury" to the immigrants.

On May 14, King issued a temporary restraining order preventing deportations until he could fully hear arguments from lawyers who claimed as many as 40,000 Nicaraguans and other immigrants had been illegally stripped of their immigration rights under the government's interpretation of new laws.

On June 12, after hearing hours of arguments, King said he could not immediately rule on a request for an injunction against deportation, effectively allowing the restraining order to expire and permitting the United States to resume deportations.
But the Immigration and Naturalisation Service vowed there would be no mass deportations and said it would await King's ruling.

The new immigration laws enacted in April left thousands of Miami immigrants, primarily Nicaraguans, living in fear. Lawyers said many pulled their children out of school and were moving from house to house to avoid deportation.
Ira Kurzban, a lawyer for the immigrants, hailed the ruling, calling it a "major victory."

"This decision will not only have a direct and immediate impact on tens of thousands of people here, but will influence the fate of hundreds of thousands of Salvadorans, Guatemalans, Nicaraguans and others throughout the United States," Kurzban said in a statement. "It is an historic and monumental decision."
